chapter_intro_summary: The chapter starts with three different assistant tasks: describe visible activity, read letters in an image, and understand a spoken question. It contrasts the earlier small from-scratch project with adapting an already trained image/text model. The chapter map puts use first, preparation/training next, then task-specific answer checks and a capability card. Short Python demonstrations run on CPU without loading the full model; the introduction explains GPU as a processor for many simultaneous computations. I read this introduction for context for 20.9 and did not review 20.1.
reader_summary: Recognizing the nouns in a picture does not settle what a person is doing or how objects relate. Two scenes can contain the same person and bicycle while one person rides and the other stands beside the bicycle. The handwritten cards make this concrete: both noun sets match, but only the first activity matches the written riding label. The text then explains how a real answer should satisfy the particular question, permit equivalent wording, and avoid extra claims about intentions that the photograph cannot show. Holding the question and prior dialogue fixed while replacing the actual pixels is a limited check that the answer follows the picture; a few pairs do not establish general ability.

terminology.details: 物件 answers what is present; 動作 answers what is happening; 關係 answers where/how objects connect, all explicitly explained. 集合 is described as ignoring noun order. 像素 means the actual image input, contrasted locally with typing object names into the prompt. The introduction expands MoE and CPU/GPU in context. No mathematical formula occurs in 20.9; in the code == is equality comparison, objects/activity are field names, truth is the hand-written reference, and indices 0/1 label the two cards. The small local gloss gaps for history and held-out photos are recorded in n2 and do not prevent the local exercise.

examples.details: The personally viewed A/B drawing makes the shared noun list and different poses immediately visible and identifies itself as artificial. The cats example separates a count question, a posture question, and an unsupported intention; I understand why a longer answer can add error. I have not claimed to see the actual cat photo. Changing only the real picture while holding the wording/dialogue fixed is a comprehensible comparison, and the prose explicitly limits its generalization.

program_explanation.details: The one fence supplies truth with two nouns and riding as the activity, and two cards with the same nouns but different activity strings. The loop examines each card with its number, prints equality of the noun sets, then equality of the activity. I predicted four lines: card 0 objects True/activity True; card 1 objects True/activity False. The exact fence executed in the existing .venv CPU process and matched that prediction. The prose explicitly says this code does not read an image and that real natural-language scoring cannot demand identical wording. No model execution or benchmark was inferred from the short equality test.

exercise.details: For the stated scene 有人拿著杯子, my object question is 畫面裡有哪些物件？ with answer 人和杯子. A corresponding unsupported guess is 這個杯子是他昨晚買的. My relation question is 人與杯子是什麼關係？ with answer 人拿著杯子. Its unsupported guess is 他準備把杯子送給朋友. To check them, identify whether the requested fact is an object or a visible relation, then reject the purchase history and future intention because neither follows from the provided scene. No actual cup photo was supplied, so this response uses only the exercise’s described visible fact.

necessary_prerequisites.reader_summary: Seeing a person, cup and table does not tell whether the person holds the cup or where the cup is. Swapping red/blue positions inside one averaging cell leaves the mean the same and loses left/right information. A full sequence can preserve information without proving natural-photo understanding. Object detection boxes are locally defined as rectangles locating objects. The prerequisite’s program output 128/True/False was cited by its prose, not executed by me. I used the illustration and explanation, not a model or measured output.
